newsitem.title: USA: Flawed windows may delay U.S. shuttle launch.
newsitem.headline: Flawed windows may delay U.S. shuttle launch.

text.p: Shuttle Columbia faces a launch delay after NASA decided on Friday to replace two potentially flawed cockpit windows, officials said.
Shuttle managers decided to replace the outer panes of the shuttle orbiter's two front windows because of the risk they might break during launch.

Columbia was scheduled for lift-off on Nov. 8 but that was now in doubt, said NASA spokesman Rob Navias. "It is likely that there will be a few days' delay," he said. "We'll know Engineers were concerned that the window panes had been weakened on previous missions and could fracture during a period of maximum stress, which usually occurs about one minute after launch.

The two potentially flawed windows, which are 0.6 inches (1.5 cm) thick, had flown seven and eight times before. They had been expected to last longer but engineers recently discovered worrying sub-surface cracks in windows that had flown many times.
Columbia was due to be attached to its external fuel tank and solid rocket boosters on Monday, but will now remain in its hangar for at least eight days while the suspect windows are replaced.
The shuttle's launch, originally scheduled for Oct. 31, was already delayed once because threatening hurricanes delayed rocket booster assembly work.
During Columbia's 16-day mission, a crew of five astronauts plan to release two free-flying satellites and make spacewalks to test space station construction techniques.
Also on Friday, NASA said an investigation had began to determine how a multimillion-dollar shuttle manoeuvring rocket pod was damaged on Thursday by water from a fire sprinkler system.
